---
title: "Apply Configuration"
---

Use this page after completing [Install OS](install_os.html), both for initial
configuration and for subsequent reconfiguration. Ansible makes the setup
repeatable, reviewable, and easier to share across the team.

This workflow is tested/supported on **Fedora Workstation 44 x86_64**. The
playbook gathers platform facts first and stops with the detected platform if
the distribution, major version, or architecture is unsupported.

```sh
make configure
```

`make configure` is the canonical command. It first installs the required packages, including
`ansible-core`, Python prerequisites, and `dnf-plugins-core`. It then installs
or updates the pinned Ansible Galaxy collections from `requirements.yml` and
runs the main workstation playbook through the `lab-stack` target. You do not
need to install Ansible separately.
Both workflows rely on Ansible and documented package policy rather than manual, undocumented changes.
For a workstation with user- or machine-specific automation, apply this shared
baseline first and then apply a separate [personal overlay](personal_overlays.html).

Ansible playbooks are designed to be **idempotent**: 
they describe the desired final state of the workstation.
When you rerun the command, Ansible checks what is already installed or configured and only applies missing or changed steps.
Ansible converges the machine toward that declared state, so a repeated run
should leave already-correct state unchanged. This makes the same command useful
after an interrupted run or after changing documented configuration.

`make setup` performs only prerequisite and Galaxy collection setup. It is
available for troubleshooting, but normally does not need to be called manually.

## Update and reapply configuration

Use the complete maintenance workflow when repository and installed software
versions should also be refreshed:

```sh
make update
```

In order, this command:

1. runs `git pull --ff-only` on a branch, or preserves a detached checkout and
   prints a notice;
2. refreshes Fedora packages with `sudo dnf upgrade --refresh`;
3. refreshes Flatpak applications with `flatpak update`;
4. runs the same `make configure` workflow described above; and
5. runs `make audit`.

The update stops when a step fails. It does not switch a detached checkout to a
branch or newer tag. Fedora and Flatpak prompts remain interactive so that you
can review consequential changes.

::: {.callout-manual}
**🔧 Manual setup and configuration**

After the automated installation, complete only the manual steps for software you use:

- Set up GitHub SSH/GPG identity and workstation basics in [Baseline](baseline.html).
- Log out and back in before testing Docker group access; see [Docker](docker.html).
- Configure browsers and extensions in [Chrome](chrome.html) if needed.
- Create or open a database and pair KeePassXC-Browser in [KeePassXC](keepassxc.html).
- Configure Thunderbird accounts and extensions in [Thunderbird](thunderbird.html) if needed.
- Sign in to editors, extensions, and settings sync in [VS Code](vscode.html) if needed.
- Start or verify local research services in [GROBID](grobid.html) and [LanguageTool](languagetool.html) if you use them.
- Configure OCR workflows in [OCR](ocr.html) and Quarto publishing in [Quarto](quarto.html) if relevant.
- Choose between the default TinyTeX installation and the full Fedora TeX Live installation in [LaTeX](latex.html) if needed.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Advanced: explicit commands and tags" collapse=true}

Run only one playbook tag when you need to test or reapply a specific area:

```sh
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags baseline
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags desktop_apps
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags git
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags borg_vorta
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags dropbox
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags nemo
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags veracrypt
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags ocr
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags virtualbox
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags docker
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags ocr_containers
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags development_containers
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags grobid
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags languagetool
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags latex
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags quarto
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags rstudio
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags keepassxc
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags okular
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags chrome
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags vscode
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags teams
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags thunderbird
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags thunderbird_mcp
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags desktop
```

You can also combine tags, for example:

```sh
ansible-playbook -i inventory -K playbooks/lab-stack.yml --tags keepassxc,chrome
```
:::
